content: In thermodynamics, the fundamental thermodynamic relation is a mathematical expression that combines the first and second laws of thermodynamics into a single, concise equation. This relation is expressed as follows: Here, ( E ) represents the internal energy, ( T ) is the temperature, ( S ) is the entropy, ( P ) is the pressure, and ( V ) is the volume. However, since ( U ), ( S ), and ( V ) are thermodynamic state functions, the above relation also holds for irreversible changes. If the system includes additional external variables beyond just the volume, or if the number of particles in the system can change, the fundamental thermodynamic relation generalizes to: Here, ( X_i ) are the generalized forces corresponding to the external variables ( x_i ), and ( mu_j ) are the chemical potentials associated with particles of type ( j ). Derivation Using the Microcanonical Ensemble The above derivation can be critiqued because it merely partitions the change in internal energy into heat and work in terms of entropy. Without defining entropy based on the fundamental properties of the system, the fundamental law of thermodynamics lacks substantive meaning. The entropy of an isolated system containing a specific amount of energy is defined as: [ S = k_B log Omega(E) ] Here, ( Omega(E) ) is the number of quantum states within a small energy interval between ( E ) and ( E + Delta E ). The interval ( Delta E ) is macroscopically small and kept fixed. Strictly speaking, this definition implies that entropy depends on the choice of ( Delta E ). However, in the thermodynamic limit (i.e., for an infinitely large system), the specific entropy (entropy per unit volume or per unit mass) becomes independent of ( Delta E ). Entropy, therefore, quantifies the uncertainty about the exact quantum state of the system, given that its energy lies within an interval of size ( Delta E ). The fundamental assumption of statistical mechanics is that all ( Omega(E) ) states are equally probable. This assumption allows us to derive all thermodynamic quantities of interest. The temperature is defined as: [ frac{1}{k_B T} equiv beta equiv frac{d log Omega(E)}{dE} ] For justification of this definition, refer to the relevant derivations. Suppose the system has an external parameter ( x ) that can be varied. In general, the energy eigenstates of the system will depend on ( x ). According to the adiabatic theorem of quantum mechanics, if the change in ( x ) is infinitely slow, the system remains in the same energy eigenstate, and its energy changes according to the variation in the energy of that eigenstate. The generalized force ( X ) corresponding to the external variable ( x ) is defined such that ( X dx ) represents the work performed by the system when ( x ) is increased by an amount ( dx ). For example, if ( x ) is the volume, then ( X ) is the pressure. The generalized force for a system known to be in energy eigenstate ( E_r ) is given by: [ X = -frac{partial E_r}{partial x} ] Since the system can occupy any energy eigenstate within the interval ( Delta E ), the generalized force for the system is defined as the expectation value of the above expression: [ langle X rangle = -frac{partial log Omega(E)}{partial x} ] To evaluate this average, we partition the ( Omega(E) ) energy eigenstates by counting how many of them have a value for ( frac{partial E_r}{partial x} ) within a range between ( Y ) and ( Y + Delta Y ). Now, consider changing ( x ) to ( x + dx ). The number of quantum states ( Omega(E) ) will change because the energy eigenstates depend on ( x ), causing states to move into or out of the range between ( E ) and ( E + Delta E ). Focusing on the energy eigenstates for which ( frac{partial E_r}{partial x} ) lies within the range ( Y ) to ( Y + Delta Y ), these states increase in energy by ( Y dx ). All such states within the interval ( E Y dx ) to ( E ) move from below ( E ) to above ( E ). The number of such energy eigenstates is given by: [ N_Y(E) ] If ( Y dx leq Delta E ), all these states will move into the range between ( E ) and ( E + Delta E ), contributing to an increase in ( Omega(E) ). The number of states that move from below ( E + Delta E ) to above ( E + Delta E ) is given by ( N_Y(E + Delta E) ). The difference between these two contributions represents the net change in ( Omega(E) ). If ( Y dx ) exceeds ( Delta E ), some energy eigenstates will move from below ( E ) to above ( E + Delta E ). These states are counted in both ( N_Y(E) ) and ( N_Y(E + Delta E) ), so the above expression remains valid in this case. In the thermodynamic limit, the last term scales inversely with system size and vanishes, leaving the dominant contributions to the generalized force.
